definition: How a supplier such as TSMC or an HBM maker divides scarce output among customers, usually favouring the largest, earliest and most reliable buyers. In AI hardware it can matter more than having the better design.

TSMC's panel-level version of CoWoS that builds packages on large square panels instead of round 300 mm wafers, wasting less area as packages grow. Piloting in 2026; volume not expected before 2H 2028.

Intel's Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge: small silicon bridges set into the package substrate to link dies and memory, offered as an alternative to TSMC's CoWoS; EMIB-T adds through-silicon vias for HBM.
The multilayer organic base (made with Ajinomoto Build-up Film) on which a GPU package sits and which routes thousands of connections to the board; supplied by firms such as Ibiden and Unimicron.

Graphics memory chips soldered around a processor on the board. Cheaper and simpler than HBM but with far less bandwidth per watt and per square millimetre; NVIDIA's data-center GPUs used it before P100.

The months-long process in which a GPU maker tests a supplier's HBM stacks for speed, heat, power and yield inside its own package before buying in volume. Failing it can lock a supplier out of a generation.
The enhanced version of HBM4 expected in volume from 2027, with faster pins (targets up to ~12.8 Gb/s), up to 16-high stacks of ~48-64 GB and increasingly customer-specific base dies.
The bottom logic die of an HBM stack that talks to the GPU and manages the DRAM layers above. From HBM4 it can be made on a logic process (e.g. TSMC N3P or N12), letting buyers customise it.
A multi-year supply contract that fixes volumes and often prices or price formulas, sometimes with prepayments; memory makers used them in 2026 to book HBM and DRAM output years ahead.

Low-power DRAM originally designed for phones, sold as chips or modules. Much cheaper per gigabyte and denser than HBM but with far lower bandwidth; used for large-capacity inference cards such as Qualcomm's AI200.
Sharing a large bank of memory among many processors over a fabric such as CXL or Ethernet, so capacity can be added without buying more GPUs or HBM.
A period when memory demand outruns supply and prices and margins rise sharply across DRAM and HBM, as in 2026 when DRAM industry revenue rose 81% in one quarter.

How many billions of bits each wire of a memory interface carries per second (Gb/s). HBM bandwidth per stack = interface width x pin speed / 8; Rubin's HBM4 revision traces to lower-than-targeted pin speeds.
Cash a buyer pays a supplier in advance to reserve future capacity or output; it sits on the buyer's balance sheet as a prepaid asset and can be lost if demand collapses.

Static RAM: very fast memory built into the processor die itself. It offers huge bandwidth but little capacity per square millimetre, so SRAM-first chips (Groq, Cerebras, d-Matrix) trade capacity for speed.
